answer:
**The distinction concerns how model capacity grows as data grows.** A parametric model has a fixed-size parameterization once its architecture is specified. Linear regression with d features has d slopes and an intercept whether trained on 100 or a million examples. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

Logistic regression and a Gaussian mixture with a fixed number of components are further parametric examples. A fixed neural-network architecture is also parametric despite having many weights.

KNN retains a growing set of examples. Kernel density estimation typically places a contribution at each observation. An unrestricted decision tree can add more regions as more data arrives. These are common nonparametric examples.

**Neither category is assumption-free.** KNN assumes the chosen distance makes nearby examples informative; density estimation depends on bandwidth; trees depend on partitioning rules. A fixed leaf cap also restricts a tree's capacity. Conversely, a very large parametric model can be extremely flexible. Choose based on sample efficiency, computational cost, and inductive bias rather than interpreting “nonparametric” as “no parameters” or “always more general.”

**Technical details and references.**

A parametric model has a fixed-size parameterization under a specified architecture as sample size grows: linear regression, logistic regression, and a fixed-component Gaussian mixture are examples. Nonparametric model complexity can grow with data: kNN, kernel density estimation, and unconstrained-depth decision trees are examples. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

The distinction is about model capacity/representation, not whether parameters exist. A neural network with a fixed architecture is parametric despite many weights. A tree with a fixed leaf cap has a capacity restriction. Both families require assumptions and regularization; “nonparametric” does not mean assumption-free.
